accroche: In 1961, two anthropologists are supposed to record genealogies to support the hypothesis of a hereditary kuru. Their records contradict it.
contenu_vulgarise:
In July 1961, Shirley Lindenbaum and Robert Glasse began a survey among the Fore, in the New Guinea highlands, with a precise assignment. Their funding came from a Rockefeller Foundation grant obtained by Henry Bennett of the University of Adelaide, one of the first to propose a genetic explanation for kuru. Bennett asked them to study Fore kinship and to gather the genealogies that, he thought, would confirm his theory.

Kuru was then a medical enigma. Described by medicine in the mid-1950s, it struck mainly women and children. Brain tissue was progressively destroyed and death came within 6 to 12 months, with no fever and no inflammation: nothing suggested an infectious agent. Between 1957 and 1977, about 2,500 people died of it, most of them adult Fore women. In 1962, among 125 men over 21 in Wanitabe, 63 no longer had a living wife.

## What the Records Show

First, the genealogies did not look like genetic trees. Many victims were not related by blood: the Fore readily adopt, create kin through a formal shared meal at midday, and their genealogies do not reach back more than five generations. Second, the accounts collected village by village traced a path. According to the Fore, kuru entered their territory around 1920 from Uwami, a village in the northwest, then reached Wanitabe around 1930 and certain areas in the south in the 1940s. Deaths were concentrated among young adults and their parents, and were very rare in the previous generation. This contradicted a purely genetic model, which assumed a very ancient origin and a stable disease.

## A Funeral Rite

The mode of spread remained to be explained. The Fore practiced mortuary endocannibalism: relatives consumed the body of the deceased. Lindenbaum and Glasse noted that this consumption involved mainly adult women, children of both sexes, and a few men, since boys left this female world for the men's house around age 10. This profile overlaps with that of the victims. The Fore knew how to name those who had died of kuru and those who had taken part in the meal.

Their conclusions received little attention, often skeptical, until 1966. That year, Gajdusek, Gibbs, and Alpers published in Nature the transmission of a kuru-like syndrome to chimpanzees inoculated with brain tissue from patients; according to the 1976 Nobel Prize press release, the inoculation dates from 1965 and the first symptoms appeared 18 months to 3 years later. After the practice was abandoned, kuru disappeared among children and the age of patients rose. Gajdusek shared the 1976 Nobel Prize in Medicine with Baruch Blumberg.

## An Assignment That Backfires

The original commission was to confirm a hypothesis with genealogies. The genealogies, recorded honestly, refuted it, because they described Fore kinship as it was: social as much as biological. Some physicians were looking for a hereditary cause; the fieldwork found a path of contagion running through ties of shared meals.

The story does not end in the 1960s. In 2006, a team published in The Lancet eleven cases of kuru identified from 1996 to 2004, all in people born before the end of cannibalism in the 1950s. The authors estimate that incubation in men lasted 39 to 56 years, and perhaps seven more, which brings the possible incubation period of a human prion disease to more than 50 years.

carte.punch: They asked for genealogies to support a hereditary kuru. The genealogies contradicted the hypothesis.
carte.idee: In 1961, Lindenbaum and Glasse record Fore kinship to confirm a genetic hypothesis. Their records show a disease that arrived around 1920 and was tied to funeral meals. In 1966, inoculated chimpanzees confirm transmission.
carte.source_courte: Lindenbaum, Phil. Trans. R. Soc. B, 2008

quiz.question: What do Lindenbaum and Glasse's field records show about kuru?
choix: That the disease struck mainly the families closest by blood, which confirmed heredity
That many victims were not related by blood and that the disease had advanced from village to village
That the disease had existed among the Fore for centuries, at a stable frequency
That the victims had all eaten the same local plant, pointing to poisoning
quiz.explication: Fore kinship was in large part social (adoption, shared meals), and kuru had reached their territory around 1920 along a route the villagers could describe: this contradicted the assumed heredity and antiquity. No record pointed to a plant, and the frequency was not stable.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Why does Henry Bennett fund the field survey entrusted to Lindenbaum and Glasse in 1961?
choix: He hopes the genealogies recorded will confirm his hypothesis of a hereditary kuru
He wants to check whether kuru is transmitted by direct contact between patients
He seeks to map the distribution of Fore language groups
He wants to test an experimental treatment on Fore patients
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Bennett, of the University of Adelaide, is one of the first to have proposed a genetic explanation for kuru. He obtains the Rockefeller grant and asks Lindenbaum and Glasse to gather genealogies that, he thinks, will confirm this hereditary theory.

quiz_supplementaire.question: According to the entry, what clinical feature of kuru made the disease baffling to 1950s medicine?
choix: It struck almost exclusively young men returning from hunting
It caused intense fever and inflammation, with no visible destruction of the brain
It progressively destroyed brain tissue and killed within six to twelve months, with no fever and no inflammation
It was transmitted only by insect bite, according to the first medical hypotheses
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Kuru progressively destroyed brain tissue and killed within six to twelve months, with no fever and no inflammation, which suggested no known infectious agent. It struck mainly women and children, not young hunters.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does the article by Gajdusek, Gibbs, and Alpers published in Nature in 1966 contribute?
choix: Proof that kuru is a hereditary disease passed between Fore generations
The final count of the 2,500 people who died of kuru between 1957 and 1977
The description of the Fore funeral rite recorded by Lindenbaum and Glasse
The transmission of a kuru-like syndrome to chimpanzees inoculated with brain tissue from patients
quiz_supplementaire.explication: In 1966, Gajdusek, Gibbs, and Alpers published in Nature the transmission of a kuru-like syndrome to chimpanzees inoculated with brain tissue from patients, which finally gave an audience to the conclusions of Lindenbaum and Glasse, received until then with skepticism.
